title: Position: Benchmarks Do Not Measure Deployment Readiness in Clinical AI
claim: Benchmarks should only filter candidate models; deployment readiness needs prospective studies and monitoring, since benchmark scores and real-world utility diverge.
layout: 3 panels: top left-to-right pipeline, bottom wheel and 2x2 quadrant
description: The figure has three panels. Panel (a), across the top, is a left-to-right pipeline with hollow arrows between stages. A cluster of robot icons (candidate models) goes into a funnel labeled 'Filtering to Select Strong Models'. A red brace and red text below the funnel read 'Optimizing for Benchmark Performance'. The pipeline continues through prospective studies, real-world evidence (a red cross with a magnifier), continuous monitoring (a looping magnifier), an ellipsis, and finally 'Confidence in Clinical Utility' (a thumbs-up shield). Panel (b), bottom left, is a pie wheel with 'Clinical Utility' at the center. Its eight spokes each have an icon: patient outcomes, cost, privacy, patient experience, decision quality, equity, safety and workflow. Panel (c), bottom right, is a 2x2 plot of benchmark performance against clinical utility. An orange dashed box marks models that provide value, and a blue dashed box marks models that benchmarks select. The quadrants include 'Quiet Workhorses' and 'Good on Paper, Bad in Practice'.
caption: Beyond Benchmarking: Toward Clinically Useful AI Models.
abstract: Despite large language models (LLMs) achieving impressive performance on benchmark tasks such as medical question answering, their real-world utility remains limited. We argue that while benchmarks play a valuable role in developing methods and filtering promising models during development, they often tell us very little about deployment readiness. Many health AI systems with strong retrospective accuracy have failed in practice, while others with modest benchmark performance have demonstrated meaningful clinical benefits. We detail the limitations of benchmark-centric evaluations of deployment readiness. We argue that we should only use benchmarks to find candidate methods or models, not to justify deployment. We call for increased use of prospective studies and policy changes that align incentives with clinically grounded evaluation.
